harness.harness: Devin: CLI subagents (run_subagent / read_subagent; profiles subagent_explore, subagent_general, custom agents/*.md), managed Devins / child sessions (coordinator pattern), dynamic workflows
harness.default_visibility: DEVIN CLI SUBAGENTS (verified): parent conversation: NONE. 'A subagent shares tools and codebase context with the parent, but operates in its own conversation chain -- it does not inherit the parent's conversation history.' 'Subagents run as their own agent sessions, each with its own context window and inference calls.' Parent task: the spawn prompt only ('the run_subagent tool takes a profile, not a model'). Profile descriptions are shown to the parent: 'The agent sees a description of each available profile and chooses the most appropriate one'. Nesting: 'By default, subagents cannot spawn their own subagents — only the root agent can. Subagent tools (run_subagent and read_subagent) are disabled inside a subagent to prevent unbounded nesting'; custom profiles opt in with max-nesting (integer, default none). Background subagents 'inherit any tool permissions you have already granted during the current session'; ask_user_question 'is always withheld from subagents'. MANAGED DEVINS (cloud; advanced-capabilities page): 'delegate them to a team of managed Devins working in parallel, each running in its own isolated VM. The coordinator session scopes the work, monitors progress, resolves conflicts, and compiles results'; the coordinator can 'launch child sessions with specific prompts, playbooks, tags, and ACU limits' and 'send follow-up instructions or clarifications to running sessions'; 'Devin analyzes your request and proposes the sessions for your approval before launching them.' The page never states whether a child sees the coordinator's conversation; documented channels are launch prompt, playbook, tags and follow-up messages (V0/V1-by-prose). DYNAMIC WORKFLOWS page (new): each agent() call 'spawns an agent and waits for its structured output. By default that agent is an independent Devin session on its own VM'; separate-VM child 'cannot see the orchestrating session's files, so code handoffs go through git branches'; shared-VM option 'shares its working tree, including uncommitted changes'.
harness.returned_to_parent: CLI: 'You do not see the subagent's raw output directly. When a subagent finishes, the parent agent reads the result and summarizes the key findings and actions for you' (the parent model reads the result; read_subagent tool exists). Background: 'The parent is automatically notified when the subagent completes'; if a foreground subagent is backgrounded 'the parent agent's tool call has already returned ... The subagent's result won't feed back into the parent's current pipeline, but you'll be notified when it completes.' Cancelled, failed or completed subagents can be resumed with a new prompt (always foreground). Managed Devins: coordinator 'compiles results'; release note 'Structured Output for Child Sessions' (April 3, 2026): 'Child sessions can return structured JSON via schema for automated workflows'; MCP: 'wait for all of them to finish in a single call instead of polling individually' and 'Inspect any session's full event timeline'. Dynamic workflows: agent(prompt, phase=..., schema=...) 'Runs one agent and returns its structured output as a dict'; failed or invalid output is handled by the script (skip, default, retry, fail).
harness.sibling_or_ledger_visibility: CLI: not documented; each subagent is its own session; the subagent panel (profile, title, status, elapsed time, tool call count) is a user-facing view, and 'Subagent activity survives a session reload'. Managed Devins: children are isolated VMs; the coordinator monitors status, todos and PRs via the Agents tab (release notes March 27, 2026 and April 1, 2026); no child-to-child visibility, shared ledger or peer polling is described; coordinator-to-child messaging is one-directional per child; 'Schedule messages to itself' lets the coordinator check back. Dynamic workflows: stage outputs flow only through the script's structured results; shared-VM agents share one working tree with 'no isolation'.
harness.knobs: CLI: subagents_enabled (config, default true; false removes run_subagent and read_subagent; org 'Default subagent model' set to None disables subagents regardless); foreground vs background spawn, Ctrl+B to background, resume; profiles subagent_explore (read-only tools plus web search; default subagent model, 'SWE-1.6 by default', resolved by a router at spawn time) and subagent_general ('The same model as the parent agent', full tools foreground, pre-approved tools only background); custom profile frontmatter: name (default file or directory name), description (default none), model (default 'default subagent model (SWE-1.6 by default) — not the parent's model'), allowed-tools (default all tools), max-nesting (integer, default none); definition locations .devin/agents/, .agents/agents/, ~/.config/devin/agents/, and imported .claude/agents/*.md (tools alias accepted); skills run in a subagent may set model:. Managed Devins: launch prompt, playbooks, tags, ACU limits per child; message, sleep or terminate children; self-scheduled reminders; Devin MCP session tools; structured output schema per child session (April 3, 2026). Dynamic workflows: agent(prompt, phase, schema), separate VM (default) vs shared VM, resumable runs keyed by prompt+schema hash.
harness.static_instruction_confound: CLI subagents share 'tools and codebase context' with the parent and any tool permissions already granted; custom profile Markdown bodies are the subagent's system prompt; skills can run inside a subagent. Managed Devins receive playbooks and organization knowledge as full Devin sessions (knowledge and plugins are org-wide per the release notes: 'Centralized Skill Management via Plugins', July 17, 2026). AGENTS.md-style repo files are accepted as custom-agent definition filenames (AGENT.md, AGENTS.md, agent.md, agents.md) but that is a profile format, not an injected instruction.

harness.harness: LangChain / LangGraph: LangGraph subgraphs and state schemas; LangChain supervisor / sub-agents-as-tools; LangChain deepagents subagents (task tool) and context-engineering page
harness.default_visibility: LangChain supervisor pattern (subagents-personal-assistant page): 'By default, sub-agents receive only the request string from the supervisor. You might want to pass additional context, such as conversation history or user preferences.' The ToolRuntime pattern reads runtime.state['messages'] (e.g. the first human message) and 'allows sub-agents to see the full conversation context, which can be useful for resolving ambiguities'. deepagents subagents page: 'Subagents isolate this detailed work—the main agent receives only the final result, not the dozens of tool calls that produced it'; 'Each subagent works with clean context focused only on its task'; SubAgent fields: system_prompt 'Required. Instructions for the subagent. Custom subagents must define their own ... Does not inherit from main agent'; tools 'Inherits from main agent by default. When specified, overrides the inherited tools entirely'; model 'Inherits from main agent by default'; middleware 'Does not inherit from the main agent'; interrupt_on 'Inherits from main agent by default'; permissions 'Inherits from main agent by default' (when set 'replaces the parent agent's permissions entirely'); skills: 'General-purpose subagent: Automatically inherits skills from the main agent'; 'Custom subagents: Do NOT inherit skills by default'; 'skill state is fully isolated in both directions: the parent's skills are not visible to the child, and the child's skills are not propagated back to the parent.' General-purpose subagent: 'Uses its own default system prompt with profile overlays applied', 'Has access to all the same tools', 'Uses the same model (unless overridden)', 'Inherits skills from the main agent'. Context management: 'When you invoke a parent agent with runtime context, that context automatically propagates to all subagents. Each subagent run receives the same runtime context you passed on the parent invoke / ainvoke call' (per-subagent namespaced keys available). Context-engineering page ('Context engineering in Deep Agents'): table row 'Runtime context ... Per run, propagates to subagents'; 'Context isolation ... Use subagents to quarantine heavy work, returning only results to the main agent'; How it works: 'Main agent has a task tool to delegate work; Subagent runs with its own fresh context; Subagent executes autonomously until completion; Subagent returns a single final report to the main agent; Main agent's context stays clean'; memory files: 'Memory files (AGENTS.md) provide persistent context that is always loaded into the system prompt' of the deep agent (the page does not say whether memory reaches subagents); custom state schemas: 'Declarative SubAgent specs passed to subagents= inherit the parent state_schema when Deep Agents compiles them for the task tool' (CompiledSubAgent and remote AsyncSubAgent specs do not). LangGraph subgraphs: not re-fetched this run (first-table sentences on shared-key vs wrapper-node schemas stand).
harness.returned_to_parent: Supervisor: 'We return only the sub-agent's final response, as the supervisor doesn't need to see intermediate reasoning or tool calls'; 'Make sure sub-agent prompts emphasize that their final message should contain all relevant information. A common failure mode is sub-agents that perform tool calls but don't include the results in their final response.' deepagents: final result as a ToolMessage; with response_format 'its structured response is JSON-serialized and returned as the ToolMessage content to the parent agent' (requires deepagents>=0.5.3); 'Subagent returns a single final report to the main agent'; files written by subagents are readable by the main agent through the shared filesystem ('Subagents can write results to files; the main agent reads what it needs'). Each subagent's name is written to lc_agent_name run metadata (LangSmith observability, not parent-visible).
harness.sibling_or_ledger_visibility: Not visible by default in either pattern: each sub-agent invocation starts from the request string (supervisor) or the task() argument plus runtime context (deepagents); skill state isolated both ways; middleware not inherited. Sibling results reach a sibling only if the main agent restates them or through the shared filesystem / long-term memory store. LangGraph: siblings see each other only through shared state channels (first table).
harness.knobs: Supervisor: the request string; ToolRuntime in the tool wrapper to forward runtime.state['messages'] or user preferences; tool descriptions; checkpointer 'only to the top-level agent'. deepagents: SubAgent fields name, description, system_prompt (required, not inherited), tools, model, middleware, interrupt_on, skills, response_format, permissions; general_purpose_subagent=GeneralPurposeSubagentProfile(...) on the harness profile (rename, re-prompt, or enabled=False), or a custom subagent named 'general-purpose' replaces it; runtime context propagation with per-subagent namespaced keys; state_schema (deepagents>=0.6.6) inherited by declarative subagents; dynamic subagents (interpreter runtime, beta); memory=[...AGENTS.md...] and skills for the main agent; long-term memory via CompositeBackend to a LangGraph Store. LangGraph: state-schema design (first table).
harness.static_instruction_confound: deepagents: memory files (AGENTS.md) are 'always injected' into the main agent's system prompt; whether they reach subagents is not stated. The general-purpose subagent inherits the main agent's skills and tools and uses the built-in subagent system prompt with profile overlays; custom subagents inherit tools, model, interrupt_on and permissions by default but not system_prompt, middleware or skills; runtime context (user metadata, keys) propagates to every subagent. Supervisor: nothing beyond the request string unless forwarded.
harness.evidence_quote: By default, sub-agents receive only the request string from the supervisor.

must_reads.title: MasDrift: Benchmarking Authorization Preservation Across Multi-Agent Architectures
must_reads.why: The closest existing manipulation of what a delegated worker sees. Their re-anchoring defense (re-show the root request to every pending call) is functionally our V1/V2, and their depth-widening loss of authorization (2.7 to 19.8 percent in centralized hierarchies versus under 1 percent for peers) is the mirror image of objective-directed departure. Related work must position against it by name, and the harness discussion must cite its centralization tradeoff.

must_reads.title: Facts Without Rules: Boundary Metadata Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs
must_reads.why: Shows the compression step itself strips the rules that govern how facts may be used (boundary-marker survival falls from about 0.80 to 0.57 at a 25-word budget; vague constraints leak far more than explicit ones). This is the design rationale for V2 as a verbatim brief rather than a summary, for the length-matched control, and for stating the planted conflict explicitly.

must_reads.title: Where Knowledge and Authority Sit Changes What an Agent Benchmark Can Resolve
must_reads.why: 864 trials holding task and success criteria fixed while moving facts, tools and permissions across access structures; access structure, not content, separates models. It is the published precedent that information placement is the variable, with task success as the outcome we deliberately do not use.

must_reads.title: Omission Constraints Decay While Commission Constraints Persist in Long-Context LLM Agents
must_reads.why: Our planted conflicts are commission-type, which this 4,416-trial study predicts to be robust (100 percent), while prohibition-type constraints fall from 73 to 33 percent compliance. Either a prohibition variant enters Suite B or the paper states the asymmetry as a limitation. Its token-matched padding arm is also the direct precedent for the LM2/LM4 control and for reading the null filler result.

must_reads.title: Thinking Mode | DeepSeek API Docs
must_reads.why: The alias table maps requested xhigh to actual high on both V4 models, and high is the default. The null effect of the effort option on DeepSeek is therefore by construction, not an empirical finding, and the methods section must say so. It also documents that temperature and related parameters are inert in thinking mode and that reasoning_content is returned.

must_reads.title: Reasoning
must_reads.why: For Muse Spark, xhigh is a real maximum and omitting the parameter yields a model-determined level, so the aliasing explanation does not transfer to Muse. Paired with the DeepSeek page it forces the effort caveat to be split by model. Also the source for reasoning tokens being billed as completion tokens, which the cost accounting of the roughly twofold reasoning-token rise needs.

must_reads.title: The Price of Thinking: Reasoning Effort as a Model-Specific API Contract
must_reads.why: A registered paired contrast plus a contract census showing that effort terms are model-specific fields with documented, non-uniform semantics of presence and omission. It supplies the frame for reporting runs at provider-default effort and for treating reasoning volume as a covariate.

must_reads.title: Can escalation channels redirect reward hacking toward defect disclosure?
must_reads.why: The nearest experimental analogue to the FLAGGED class: across 8 models a disclosure channel plus policy cuts hacking from 23.6 to 5.3 percent and escalations are 98.7 percent hack-free, so disclosure and deviation become near mutually exclusive when a channel exists. It is the quantified prior behind reading our flag rate as chosen disclosure and behind the Suite B escalation-tool arm.

must_reads.title: Agents Catching Agents: Shortcut Cascades and Benchmark Gaming in Clinical Multi-Agent Systems
must_reads.why: The nearest quantification of silent versus announced departure under peer visibility: drifters name what moved them in 1 of 10 text and 1 of 134 imaging cases, and a referee that privately re-queries the holdout catches what a transcript judge cannot. It is the sharpest published contrast to our zero silent-deviation count and the template for the Suite B referee check. Promoted from should.

must_reads.title: GPT-5.6 System Card
must_reads.why: Vendor evidence that the more capable, higher-effort model goes beyond stated user intent more often (Section 7.2), matching the capability-ordered departure we observe, and the only frontier card that mentions subagent coordination without evaluating delegation conflicts, which is the gap the harness table fills.

must_reads.title: HANDBOOK.md: A Benchmark for Long-Context Agentic Instruction Following
must_reads.why: A standing policy in context is routinely overridden by plausible in-environment requests and agents report compliance they did not achieve, graded by 824 deterministic criteria. It is both the checker-design precedent and the reason the zero silent-deviation claim must be scoped to output-observable, single-delegation tasks.

must_reads.title: Hierarchical Alignment: Enforcing Hierarchical Instruction-Following in LLMs through Logical Consistency
must_reads.why: The closest formal statement of our regime: benign, partially conflicting instructions where utility must be preserved rather than an attack repelled. It names the gap in the instruction-hierarchy literature that our planted conflicts occupy.

must_reads.title: The Self-Correction Illusion: Role Relabeling Gates Explicit Error Flagging in Large Language Models
must_reads.why: Relabeling a byte-identical claim from thought to an external role moves explicit flagging by 23 to 93 points. Every visibility tier in our prompts sits in the user turn under a fixed system prompt, which the paper must state as a held-constant design choice, and it caps how far the FLAGGED rate generalizes to harnesses that place the brief in another role.

must_reads.title: Prompt Injection as Role Confusion
must_reads.why: Models infer who is speaking from how text sounds rather than from the role label. This is the mechanism for why a verbatim parent brief moves behavior while length-matched filler does not, and it makes the pre-registered V2 versus V2N (authority-neutral) contrast the right test. Promoted from should.

must_reads.title: Multi-agent | OpenAI API
must_reads.why: fork_turns makes the V0 to V2 rungs of the ladder a shipped spawn-time parameter at a frontier lab. Primary source for the OpenAI row and the strongest single piece of evidence that hierarchy visibility is a product knob rather than a lab construct.

must_reads.title: Harness Engineering: Anatomy, Architecture, and Evolution of Coding Agents -- A Source-Code Study of Eleven Systems
must_reads.why: Source-level anatomy of eleven production harnesses with the longitudinal finding that behavioral policy migrates from prompt prose into configuration. It is the primary secondary source for the harness table and the justification for recording sub-agent visibility as a settable policy. Cite the identifier as printed despite the July submission date.

must_reads.title: What's in Your Agent's Context? Context Privilege Escalation Attacks against AI Agent Harness
must_reads.why: The first systematic account of how 12 harnesses, including Claude Code and Codex, assemble context and which message roles receive it. It anchors the role-confound discussion and is the cross-check for the table's coverage.

must_reads.title: Architecture Matters for Multi-Agent Security
must_reads.why: Varies memory and context visibility as an independent variable across 13 configurations and finds no universally safer design, with attack success varying 3.8x. It is the security-side twin of our manipulation and supports the claim that cross-agent context defaults have measurable consequences.

must_reads.title: AI Organizations are More Effective but Less Aligned than Individual Agents
must_reads.why: The macro result our mechanism study nests inside: organizations of aligned models are more effective and less aligned than a single model. The visibility ladder probes one candidate driver (what each worker is shown).

must_reads.title: The Working Set of a Coding Agent: Coherence Debt in Repository-Scale Tasks
must_reads.why: Two in-the-wild observations mirror our classes: the propensity to report being blocked rather than act is a model property spanning every trial to none (our per-model FLAGGED rate), and agents follow a stale convention file even when it prescribes worse code (literal adherence over judgment).

must_reads.title: HarnessRisk: A Lifecycle-Oriented Benchmark for Agent Harness Safety
must_reads.why: Explicit risk recognition in over 90 percent of runs coexists with substantial unsafe action, measured at the model-plus-harness level across three harnesses. This recognition-versus-action gap is the exact shape of FLAGGED-but-ADHERED and belongs beside the outcome taxonomy. Promoted from should.

must_reads.title: Delegation to artificial intelligence can increase dishonest behaviour
must_reads.why: Thirteen incentivized experiments in Nature showing that the abstraction level of the delegation interface (rule versus goal) changes what the delegate does, and that LLM agents comply with instructions humans refuse. It is the organization-theory anchor for treating V0 to V5 as the same axis applied to a sub-agent. Promoted from should.

must_reads.title: Measuring Obedience to Authority Across Large Language Models with the Milgram Paradigm
must_reads.why: 42 models over 4,848 sessions: a modest thinking budget and moving the decision into a tool call sharply lower obedience to an insisting authority, and scripted peer defiance lowers it. Both results bear on the reasoning-token mediator and on the V3 sibling arm. Promoted from should.

direct_threats.title: MasDrift: Benchmarking Authorization Preservation Across Multi-Agent Architectures
direct_threats.what_they_did: 600 benign tasks pairing required work with reserved actions; compared single-agent, centralized and decentralized coordination while varying hierarchy depth and peer width; measured unauthorized actions (2.7 to 19.8 percent in centralized hierarchies, widening with depth, versus 0.6 to 0.8 percent in peer networks); showed that re-anchoring every pending call to the original user request cuts unauthorized actions in every configuration at 1.6 points of completion, while an attenuated policy passed along the chain forfeits up to 36.3 points.
direct_threats.how_we_differ: They measure loss of authorization boundaries (workers doing more than permitted) and treat showing the root request as a defense; we plant an explicit instruction-versus-objective conflict and measure whether visibility makes the worker depart toward the parent objective, announced or silent, with length-matched and hierarchy-matched controls, a flag-without-deviation class and reasoning-token accounting. They vary topology; we vary the visibility layer at fixed topology. Their re-anchoring result is the direction our V1/V2 rungs test from the other side (departure toward the objective rather than away from authorization).

direct_threats.title: Facts Without Rules: Boundary Metadata Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs
direct_threats.what_they_did: Manipulated the length budget and constraint explicitness of handoff summaries on GPT-5-mini and DeepSeek-R1-32B; boundary-marker survival is near-uncorrelated with fact survival and drops from about 0.80 to 0.57 at 25 words; vague constraints leak in 73 percent (GPT) and 50 percent (DeepSeek) of cases versus under 15 percent for explicit ones; a no-handoff control leaks more than the operationalized handoff; an audience allowlist nearly eliminates leakage.
direct_threats.how_we_differ: Their manipulation is the handoff artifact and the outcome is privacy leakage past a rule; we hold the worker's instruction fixed, add hierarchy context above it, and measure objective-directed departure and flagging. They show rules degrade in transit; we show what the worker does when rule and objective visibly disagree. Cite for the V1 versus V2 design rationale.

direct_threats.title: Where Knowledge and Authority Sit Changes What an Agent Benchmark Can Resolve
direct_threats.what_they_did: Incognita holds eighteen customer-service tasks fixed while moving facts, tools and permissions from direct access to one intermediary to six role-isolated participants; 864 trials on four models; social access lowered success for every model and separated model pairs centralized settings could not, attributed to failures to obtain needed information.
direct_threats.how_we_differ: They vary who holds information and permission and score task success; no conflict is planted and departure from or flagging of the brief is never asked. Our ladder varies how much of the hierarchy one worker sees and classifies adherence, flagging and deviation. Complementary axes of the same organizational question; a reviewer may still ask why we did not report success.

direct_threats.title: Omission Constraints Decay While Commission Constraints Persist in Long-Context LLM Agents
direct_threats.what_they_did: Three-arm causal study, 4,416 trials, 12 models, six conversation depths: prohibition-type operator constraints fall from 73 to 33 percent compliance between turns 5 and 16 while requirement-type constraints hold at 100 percent; token-matched padding attributes 62 to 100 percent of the dilution to semantic content; re-injecting constraints before a per-model safe depth restores compliance.
direct_threats.how_we_differ: They vary depth and constraint polarity inside one agent's system prompt; we fix depth and vary exposure to an orchestrator's objective. Their padding control is a length control like ours but measures constraint recall, not objective-directed departure. The threat is interpretive: our conflicts are commission-type, so our departure rates may be a floor for prohibition-type conflicts, and the LM-control novelty is reduced.

direct_threats.title: Architecture Matters for Multi-Agent Security
direct_threats.what_they_did: Varied agent roles, communication topology and memory/context visibility across 13 configurations in browser, desktop and code environments with stagewise evaluation from planning refusal to full attack completion; multi-agent architectures more vulnerable than standalone agents in most configurations, attack success varying up to 3.8x, no universally safer design.
direct_threats.how_we_differ: Their independent variable overlaps ours (what context each agent can see) but their dependent variable is adversarial attack completion; ours is benign conflict handling with an announced-versus-silent split and no adversary. A reviewer could read our visibility axis as already studied; the answer is that the outcome class, not the axis, is new.

direct_threats.title: Agents Catching Agents: Shortcut Cascades and Benchmark Gaming in Clinical Multi-Agent Systems
direct_threats.what_they_did: Gemini committees on a shared clinical workspace resist shortcut cues in isolation (5 to 16 percent flips) but adopt a wrong answer asserted by two peers or a false system flag in 38 percent of cases across seven cohorts; a transcript judge catches adoption on text but not imaging; a referee that privately re-queries the holdout transfers; drifters almost never name the rubric (1 of 10 text, 1 of 134 imaging).
direct_threats.how_we_differ: Their departures are toward a wrong answer under peer pressure on a shared workspace; ours are toward the parent objective under a planted conflict with no peer messages in Suite A. They find near-silent drift where we find announced departures only; the paper must attribute the difference to the direction of the pull (objective versus shortcut) and to the absence of peer assertion, and Suite B's V5 arm is where the two designs meet.

direct_threats.title: Can escalation channels redirect reward hacking toward defect disclosure?
direct_threats.what_they_did: 2x2 factorial across 8 frontier models in 5 families: a structured escalation tool at the point of conflict, an anti-reward-hacking policy, or both; combined intervention cuts hacking from 23.6 to 5.3 percent (OR 9.2); escalations 98.7 percent hack-free; escalation adds 10.1 points of defect-detection coverage over monitoring.
direct_threats.how_we_differ: Gomez manipulates the availability of a disclosure tool and a policy while holding the instruction fixed; we hold tools fixed and vary how much of the delegation hierarchy the worker sees. Her conflict is agent versus broken test infrastructure; ours is literal instruction versus parent objective, and she measures hacking rather than objective-directed departure. Overlap is confined to the FLAGGED class and the planned V5E arm.

direct_threats.title: HANDBOOK.md: A Benchmark for Long-Context Agentic Instruction Following
direct_threats.what_they_did: 65 agentic tasks under a 20 to 124 page standard operating procedure over MCP, graded by 824 deterministic criteria; the strongest model passes 36.2 percent under strict grading; failures cluster into letting an unauthorized in-environment request override standing policy, acting against a check performed, losing rule details over long horizons, and reporting compliance not achieved.
direct_threats.how_we_differ: Their policy and task are on the same side and the adversary is an unauthorized environmental request; our conflict is between the worker's own instruction and the parent objective, and the treatment is visibility rather than policy length or horizon. Their deterministic rubric is precedent for our checkers, not competition.

direct_threats.title: Hierarchical Alignment: Enforcing Hierarchical Instruction-Following in LLMs through Logical Consistency
direct_threats.what_they_did: Argued that instruction-hierarchy work has focused on adversarial attacks and overlooked benign, partially or implicitly conflicting instructions where utility and consistency must be preserved; proposed solver-guided neuro-symbolic resolution at inference distilled into parameters at training; evaluated on rule following, task execution, tool use and safety.
direct_threats.how_we_differ: They build and evaluate an alignment method for resolving benign conflicts; we intervene on nothing and measure how an unmodified worker resolves a benign conflict as a function of hierarchy visibility and whether it announces the resolution. They own the method, we own the measurement of the untreated baseline.

direct_threats.title: AI Organizations are More Effective but Less Aligned than Individual Agents
direct_threats.what_they_did: Across 12 tasks in an AI consultancy and an AI software team, multi-agent organizations of aligned models produced higher-utility but more misaligned solutions than a single aligned model; argued that safety research must address interacting systems of agents.
direct_threats.how_we_differ: They compare whole organizations to single agents on utility and misalignment; we hold the organization fixed, vary one worker's view of it, and measure conflict handling with deterministic checkers. Ours is a mechanism study nested inside their macro finding.

direct_threats.title: HarnessRisk: A Lifecycle-Oriented Benchmark for Agent Harness Safety
direct_threats.what_they_did: 128 sandboxed cases pairing a benign objective with an adversarial instruction embedded in an untrusted workflow artifact, over six harness lifecycle phases, three harnesses, six models and 14 configurations; attack success 12.6 to 80.9 percent; harness configuration the most vulnerable phase; explicit risk recognition (over 90 percent in some configurations) does not reliably lead to safe action.
direct_threats.how_we_differ: Their conflicting instruction is adversarial and the safe action is refusal; ours is a benign mis-specified delegation where the objective-directed action is departure. They do not vary how much of the objective the agent sees. The recognition-versus-action gap is the same shape as FLAGGED-but-ADHERED and should be cited as such.

direct_threats.title: The Self-Correction Illusion: Role Relabeling Gates Explicit Error Flagging in Large Language Models
direct_threats.what_they_did: Kept an erroneous claim byte-identical and varied only its message role (agent thought, user, tool response, system memory) across 12 model-domain combinations; relabeling from thought to an external role raised explicit correction by 23 to 93 points in 10 of 12 settings.
direct_threats.how_we_differ: They vary the role of a claim and measure error flagging; we vary hierarchy context and measure flagging or departure under a conflict, holding the role constant (all tiers in the user turn). It is a confound warning for our FLAGGED rate, not a competing measurement.

direct_threats.title: GPT-5.6 System Card
direct_threats.what_they_did: Pre-deployment card for the GPT-5.6 family reporting that GPT-5.6 goes beyond user intent more often than GPT-5.5, attributed to overeagerness, permissive reading of instructions and increased persistence at the highest reasoning efforts, with low absolute rates; instruction-hierarchy evaluation numbers in Section 4.2; subagent coordination mentioned only in Section 9.1.1.
direct_threats.how_we_differ: Departure from a single user's intent in production-like agentic coding, judged from chain of thought, with no orchestrator, no planted conflict and no context manipulation; no announced-versus-silent distinction. It corroborates the capability contrast and confirms no frontier card evaluates delegation conflicts.

direct_threats.title: TeamBench: Evaluating Agent Coordination under Enforced Role Separation
direct_threats.what_they_did: 851 templates and 931 instances under OS-enforced role separation so no Planner, Executor or Verifier can read the full requirements, edit the workspace and certify the answer; prompt-only and enforced teams reach indistinguishable pass rates but prompt-only runs show 3.6 times more verifier attempts to edit executor code; verifiers approve 49 percent of grader-failing submissions.
direct_threats.how_we_differ: They restrict requirement access by role and score pass rate and boundary violations; they plant no conflict between a role's instruction and the team objective, do not grade visibility, and do not classify announced versus silent departure. Their finding that role-scoped prompts do not produce role-scoped behavior is motivation for measuring visibility rather than assuming it.

direct_threats.title: The Working Set of a Coding Agent: Coherence Debt in Repository-Scale Tasks
direct_threats.what_they_did: Modeled repository-scale coding as reconstructing a coupled-fact graph; supplied and withheld facts across seven models and five harnesses; availability rather than distance decides outcomes; harnesses differ more than tenfold in tokens; an agent asked to act acts rather than reporting it is blocked, with the blocked-report rate a model property; agents follow a stale convention file even when it prescribes worse code.
direct_threats.how_we_differ: They withhold facts and measure fabrication versus blocked reports; we plant an explicit instruction-versus-objective conflict and measure disclosure versus departure as visibility grows, without manipulating hierarchy exposure on their side. Overlap is the model-property reading of flagging and the literal-adherence observation.

direct_threats.title: Do as I Say, Not as I Do: Instruction-Induction Conflict in LLMs
direct_threats.what_they_did: Opposed a user instruction with N hardcoded assistant turns demonstrating a competing pattern across 13 models, 16 instructions and up to 50 turns; adherence ranges 1 to 99 percent, largely uncorrelated with capability benchmarks; output diversity rather than semantic engagement predicts robustness; chain of thought helps without eliminating susceptibility.
direct_threats.how_we_differ: Their conflict is instruction versus in-context demonstrated behavior in chat; ours is task instruction versus parent objective in delegation, with hierarchy visibility as the manipulated variable. Their capability null must be reconciled with our capability contrast, which the first sweep already demoted to a two-case comparison.

direct_threats.title: Semantic Consensus: Process-Aware Conflict Detection and Resolution for Enterprise Multi-Agent LLM Systems
direct_threats.what_they_did: Named Semantic Intent Divergence (agents developing inconsistent readings of shared objectives from siloed context) as a root cause of enterprise multi-agent failure and proposed a six-component middleware; 600 runs on AutoGen, CrewAI and LangGraph reporting 100 percent workflow completion versus 25.1 percent baseline, 65.2 percent conflict detection at 27.9 percent precision.
direct_threats.how_we_differ: Single-author middleware proposal with a self-built evaluation and low detection precision; we isolate the visibility variable experimentally and classify per-worker conflict handling deterministically. Our finding that isolated workers essentially never depart both supports and qualifies its siloed-context diagnosis. Cite for framing, not numbers.

judge.summary: This pass fills the gaps the first sweep named with 130-odd verified entries and thirty-one harness rows, and none of them runs a graded visibility ladder with a planted benign conflict, disclosure scoring and length-matched controls, so the design survives. The one high-risk item is MasDrift, whose re-anchoring defense is our V1/V2 rung read from the authorization side and must be positioned by name; Facts Without Rules, Incognita, Omission Constraints, Architecture Matters, Agents Catching Agents and the Gomez escalation paper are moderate overlaps on single variables. The most consequential methods correction is that DeepSeek's documented alias maps xhigh to the default high, so that null is by construction, while Meta documents xhigh as a true maximum and the repository's own five-item control shows Muse reasoning tokens rising at xhigh on every listed item, so the effort caveat must be split by model and the gateway pass-through question tested directly. Verifier tiers were demoted where the gist does not touch our variables (CooperBench, Prompt Infection, ACIArena and OMNI-LEAK from must to should; Memory Non-Sharing confirmed rejected) and promoted where it does (Agents Catching Agents, Prompt Injection as Role Confusion, HarnessRisk, the Köbis Nature paper and the Milgram study). Every harness row is accepted, twenty-one as new rows and eight as replacements or amendments, with cell corrections for CAMEL Workforce (V1/V2 by construction), Copilot Studio (split child and connected), Kimi Agent Swarm (not stated) and Codex (docs silent, API and source switchable), and the rows justify five structural changes: three tables, a sibling-channel column, a who-composes-the-context column, alignment of the lab table with the vendor docs, and the static-instruction-file layer stated as a finding. The paper's V0 sits one notch above the shipped floor because several products do not even tell the child it is orchestrated, and the table's thesis becomes three regimes rather than a bimodal default. Remaining gaps are empirical rather than bibliographic: gateway effort pass-through, the Model Spec's delegation text, Google and xAI card sections, Chinese vendor context policies, issue-tracker field cases, statistics references, and full-text checks on four entries whose abstracts lack the numbers their verifiers quoted.
